The supplied text explicitly addresses the status of large-scale clinical trials for microbiome interventions in cancer immunotherapy. It states that as of late 2025, 'no completed Phase III randomized trials have yet confirmed a reproducible survival benefit of microbiome-based interventions in oncology.' The authors clarify that the current evidence base relies primarily on rigorously conducted Phase I/II trials (e.g., FMT studies in melanoma showing ~40% response rates in refractory patients) and meta-analyses of these smaller cohorts. The text details specific ongoing or completed early-phase trials, such as NCT03353402 and NCT03341143 (FMT in melanoma), NCT04167137 (SYNB1891, Phase I), and NCT03637803 (MRx0518, Phase I/II), noting that while these show feasibility and immunologic plausibility, they lack the scale and definitive survival endpoints (OS/PFS) required to satisfy the gap's success criteria. The text also highlights a pooled analysis of eleven interventional studies (>800 patients) which showed improved objective response rates but moderate heterogeneity, further underscoring the absence of a definitive Phase III confirmation.

This study (TACITO trial) is an investigator-initiated, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled **phase 2a** clinical trial evaluating fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) in 50 randomized patients (45 in full analysis set) with metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) receiving pembrolizumab plus axitinib. The primary endpoint (12-month progression-free survival rate) was not met (P=0.053), though secondary endpoints showed significantly improved median PFS (24.0 vs 9.0 months, P=0.035) and objective response rate in the donor-FMT arm. The authors explicitly state this is the first RCT to investigate targeted FMT in mRCC with PFS/OS endpoints, positioning it as Phase 2a evidence rather than Phase III.
